t: WELCOME OFFER IN EXCHANGE FOR EMAIL
b: A popup or inline form that gives something of value for signing up. As researched this is not allowed for PEPTICITY. The compliant alternative is in Details.
why: Klaviyo puts standard homepage pop-up forms at 3 to 8% (vendor figures) (Klaviyo). Popupsmart's median is 0.83% of displays, with the top 10% at 3.87% or more (Popupsmart data).
how: Make the welcome gift knowledge, not a discount: "THE PEPTICITY PRIMER, free, plus GRACE'S LETTER monthly" (see #8 and #16). A money offer may only apply to things outside the Rx and pharmacy lane, such as [cosmetic topicals, if sold], branded merch, or an event ticket.
risk: STOP for any discount, gift or "welcome kit" tied to an Rx, a peptide program or the pharmacy fill (provincial inducement bans; C.01.044). Whether a discount on the clinician consult fee is allowed is a counsel question (provincial colleges of physicians may have their own inducement rules) [UNVERIFIED]. A welcome discount on unauthorized peptides is illegal.

t: FREE, DISCREET DELIVERY AS THE STANDARD (NOT A THRESHOLD)
b: Free shipping, either always or above a threshold, used as an incentive.
why: Unexpected extra costs are the top cart-abandonment reason in Baymard's research. It is reported as 39% or 48%, depending on the base, via secondary sources (Contentsquare summary).
how: Put "Discreet delivery included" on the all-in price card (#20). Never use a spend threshold on Rx. Use a threshold only on non-Rx shop items.
risk: CAUTION. Free delivery of an Rx is part of the pharmacy service and is normal practice (Felix). But "free shipping if you spend $X on prescriptions" looks like an inducement. Keep it flat and unconditional.

t: PROVINCE WAITLIST ("NOT IN YOUR PROVINCE YET")
b: Visitors outside a served area join a list to hear when service opens there.
why: A waitlist turns a dead end (wrong province) into a lead. The scarcity is real because licensure really is provincial.
how: When the quiz's province question is unserved, show "WE'RE NOT LICENSED IN [PROVINCE] YET". Ask for email and province only. Use an unticked "Also send me GRACE'S LETTER" box, kept separate from the "tell me when you open" consent.
risk: SAFE. Never publish waitlist counts unless they are real and current. Don't promise opening dates.

b: A pre-launch list that gets first booking access.
why: It gives status and first access, and it is the classiest form of urgency when the limit is real.
how: "THE FOUNDING LIST": first access to consult booking when a province or program opens, a founder's welcome letter, and an invitation to the first live session (#13). Any cap must be real, for example "[N] consult slots in the first week", tied to actual clinician hours.
risk: CAUTION. "Lifetime discounts" on Rx or pharmacy services are STOP (inducement). Perks must be access and information, not price on Rx. If there's a stated cap or deadline, honour it (Competition Bureau).

b: One-tap alerts when something comes back or opens. As researched this is not allowed for PEPTICITY. The compliant alternative is in Details.
how: Use it for consult openings ("Tell me when an evening slot opens with a clinician licensed in [province]"), new guide releases, and live-session dates.
risk: STOP for "drop alerts" on Rx drugs or peptides: that is product promotion, and for unauthorized peptides it is promoting an illegal sale. Alerts about service capacity are SAFE.

b: On mobile, a button opens the visitor's messaging app with a pre-filled text. They tap Send and are subscribed.
how: Keep two separate lanes. The first is transactional texts: appointment reminders and "your clinician's note is ready". The second is marketing texts, opt-in only and rare (a monthly "letter is out", or a new province open).
risk: CAUTION. CASL covers SMS, so you need identification, STOP handling and a consent log. Never put health details in an SMS (lock screens are visible). A transactional opt-in is not marketing consent.

t: EXIT-INTENT OR TIMED SLIDE-IN (OFFERING THE GUIDE)
b: A panel that appears when the cursor leaves the page, or after time or scroll depth.
how: One quiet frosted-glass slide-in, bottom corner on desktop and a bottom sheet on mobile. Show it once per session and at most three times ever. Offer the PRIMER (#8) or "Email me this page". Never show it over the quiz or the booking flow.
risk: SAFE if it's dismissable and offers no Rx discount.

b: A slim top bar with one current message and one link.
how: Rotate true service news: "NOW BOOKING CLINICIAN CONSULTS IN [PROVINCES]", "THE OCTOBER LETTER IS OUT: READ IT", or "LIVE Q&A [DATE]: SAVE A SEAT".
risk: SAFE. No timers, and no drug names. ---

b: A downloadable guide given for an email address.
why: A specific, named asset beats a generic "subscribe" button. Both brands lead with the asset, not with "newsletter".
how: "THE PEPTICITY PRIMER: PEPTIDE CARE IN CANADA, PLAINLY". It covers what Health Canada authorizes and what it has warned about; how a clinician consult works; what a partner pharmacy does; how to read a lot certificate (COA); questions to bring (#12); and pricing explained in CAD.
risk: CAUTION. No benefit claims ("heals", "boosts", "supports"), no dosing, cycles or stacks, and no named Rx drug next to a goal. Have a regulatory read of the PDF before release, and date-stamp each edition.

b: Lessons drip-fed by email over several days.
why: It sets up a habit of opening the emails, and every lesson is a soft touchpoint before booking. Automated flows reportedly outperform campaigns by 3 to 4x (vendor) (Inboxally).
how: "FIVE DAYS TO A BETTER CONSULT". Day 1: how care works in Canada. Day 2: "research use only" explained (#15). Day 3: reading a COA. Day 4: what your clinician will ask. Day 5: real costs, then a gentle "Book when ready".
risk: SAFE with the same wording rules as #9.

b: A searchable A to Z of terms, which is an SEO magnet with an inline "email me new entries".
how: "PEPTIDE TERMS, PLAINLY": COA, HPLC, mass spec, lot number, DIN, NPN, compounding, Health Canada-authorized, research-use-only, licensed partner pharmacy.
risk: CAUTION. Define process and documentation terms, not drugs. An entry for an unauthorized peptide that reads as "what it does" would be promotion. If drug entries are ever added, give regulatory status only, with a link to the HC advisory. Terms such as "reconstitution" are defined in words only: no ratios, volumes or calculators. The peptide-expert skill notes that FDA's August 2026 letters treated a "peptide calculator" plus bacteriostatic water as evidence of intended human use [VERIFY].

b: A printable consult-prep sheet.
why: It is useful, safety-led and clinician-friendly, and it positions PEPTICITY as the careful option.
how: "YOUR CONSULT PREP SHEET": link to the ISMP 5 Questions (credited; check its licence before reproducing), plus PEPTICITY's own questions. For example: "Is this authorized by Health Canada?", "Who compounds or fills it, and where?", "What is the lot certificate?" and "What does it cost all-in?". Delivered by email, with an optional download.
risk: SAFE. The best fit for PEPTICITY's model.

b: Enter the lot number from the label and see the batch's test documentation.
why: It is proof rather than promise ("transparency with receipts", per Ritual's CIO via Modern Retail). Add a capture point: "Email me this certificate for my records".
how: "CHECK YOUR LOT": the partner pharmacy's lot documentation, showing [testing lab], [method], [date] and a platinum "DOCUMENTED" chip. Placeholder: [Your verification process].
risk: CAUTION. Only for products PEPTICITY lawfully supplies. Never say "Health Canada approved" unless true (show the DIN). A public COA for an unauthorized peptide is promotion. Confirm with the pharmacy which records it can lawfully publish.

b: A side-by-side table, downloadable, or emailed as "the full chart".
how: Compare routes, not drugs: your family doctor; a walk-in clinic; an online clinic; PEPTICITY (licensed clinician, then a licensed partner pharmacy); and "research use only" websites. Rows cover who decides, who fills, lot documentation, price clarity and privacy.
risk: CAUTION. Comparative claims must be true and provable when made (Competition Act s.74.01). Don't name competitors without counsel, and use categories instead.

b: A myth-versus-fact explainer that builds trust, with "Get the full explainer by email".
why: It sets PEPTICITY apart in a category whose buyers are wary of grey-market shops, so honesty becomes the hook.
risk: SAFE, provided it quotes Health Canada accurately and doesn't disparage named businesses. ---

t: THE QUIZ, WITH "EMAIL ME MY SUMMARY"
b: The existing routing quiz, with the result shown first and an optional email capture after it.
how: On the result page, offer "EMAIL ME THIS SUMMARY", "TEXT ME A LINK TO FINISH BOOKING LATER" and an unticked "Also send GRACE'S LETTER".
risk: SAFE as built. Keep quiz answers out of ad pixels (BetterHelp precedent), and keep health answers out of the marketing email body.

t: ALL-IN COST AND COVERAGE ESTIMATOR (NOT DOSING)
b: A calculator showing what the first one to three months cost, with "Email me this estimate".
why: Price uncertainty is a top reason people stall, and a personal estimate is worth emailing to yourself.
how: The inputs are province, consult type and membership or no membership. The output is the consult fee, pharmacy fee, delivery and tax in CAD. Add a line on claiming: "Prescription drugs may be claimable when prescribed by a practitioner and recorded by a pharmacist. Check with your plan." This is the CRA test under ITA 118.2(2)(n) (HR Reporter; Federal Court decision). Offer "We provide itemized receipts" [confirm with Grace].
risk: SAFE if it is about price only. STOP for any dose, mg or "how much do I need" logic. Don't promise that anything is claimable. ---

b: A personal, useful monthly letter, which is the anchor of the email list.
how: "GRACE'S LETTER": Canadian regulatory news in plain words (Health Canada advisories, newly authorized generics), how the pharmacy partner works, one reader question answered, and the next live session.
risk: SAFE, as long as no issue promotes a named Rx drug for an indication. Footer: identification, mailing address, one working unsubscribe.

b: An episodic show that feeds the newsletter.
how: "THE PROCESS", a 5-minute video series: a day at the partner pharmacy, how a lot is tested, what a consult covers, and how privacy is handled.
risk: CAUTION. A clinician on camera talking up a specific therapy turns content into Rx advertising (Health Canada's Distinction Guidance, cited in the earlier doc). Keep it to process and safety, and pre-review scripts.

b: Registration-based events.
how: A free virtual evening, "HOW PEPTIDE CARE WORKS IN CANADA", with Grace and a pharmacist, and pre-submitted questions only. Registration captures name, email and province, with unticked marketing consent. Send the replay link by email.
risk: CAUTION. Same rules as #19. No individual advice in a group setting ("book a consult for that"). Moderate questions.

b: A members-only list or space.
how: "THE INNER LIST" for patients: early guide releases, a seat at live sessions, and a direct line to the care coordinator.
risk: CAUTION. Peer health talk in a brand-run space can become de facto testimonials and claims. Start as an email list, not a forum. No published member counts. ---

b: Named people with credentials.
why: In an experiment summarized by the University of Nevada, Reno, identical information attributed to a doctor was trusted significantly more than when it was attributed to a blogger or actress (Hitchcock Project review). Evidence on physician photos is small and mixed (JMIR Infodemiology 2022).
how: "WHO DECIDES": [Name, licence type, province, licence number] with a link to the public college register so the visitor can verify. Placeholders until real people agree.
risk: CAUTION. Clinicians must not endorse products (check the relevant college's advertising rules) [UNVERIFIED]. Never invent people or credentials.

t: ALL-IN PRICE CARD (AND A DOWNLOADABLE PRICE SHEET)
b: One price per program showing exactly what it includes.
how: "WHAT YOU PAY, ALL IN": consult, pharmacy, delivery, renewal terms beside the button, and "Email me the price sheet".
risk: SAFE, and it is required by drip-pricing law. On the price list, name an Rx with name, price and quantity only, never with the goal.

t: LAWFUL "NOTHING TO PAY IF IT ISN'T RIGHT" PROMISE
b: A risk-reversal promise.
why: A review of 22 papers (Janakiraman et al., *J. Retailing*) found lenient return policies lift purchases, though they can also raise returns (AMA summary).
how: "IF THE CLINICIAN DECIDES IT ISN'T RIGHT FOR YOU, YOU PAY NOTHING FOR THE PROGRAM." Add a clear consult-fee and cancellation policy [confirm with Grace].
risk: STOP for an outcome guarantee like Numan's (results or money back) on an Rx in Canada. It is an implied performance claim needing proof in advance (Competition Act s.74.01(1)(b)), and it is an inducement tied to Rx use. A process guarantee (not charged if declined, easy cancellation) is SAFE.

t: THE PRIVACY PROMISE AS A HOOK
b: A visible pledge beside every form.
how: A one-line pledge under each email field: "YOUR ANSWERS NEVER GO TO AD PLATFORMS. UNSUBSCRIBE IN ONE CLICK." Link it to a plain-language privacy page.
risk: SAFE, but only if it is true. Audit the tags first. ---

b: Real-time availability, so the scarcity is true.
how: "NEXT OPENING WITH A CLINICIAN LICENSED IN [PROVINCE]: [THU 2:30 PM ET]", pulled live from the booking calendar. If it's full, show "Notify me of an opening" (#5).
risk: SAFE if it's live data. STOP for countdown timers, "only 3 spots left" that isn't true, or offers renewed after a deadline. ---

b: Existing customers invite friends. As researched this is not allowed for PEPTICITY. The compliant alternative is in Details.
why: Schmitt, Skiera & Van den Bulte (*J. Marketing* 2011, German bank, about 10,000 customers) found referred customers worth at least 16% more, with higher retention (Wharton PDF).
how: A reward-free share: "SEND A FRIEND THE PRIMER" or "SHARE THE CONSULT PREP SHEET", which captures the friend's email only if the friend opts in themselves.
risk: STOP for cash, credit or discounts tied to an Rx, a peptide program or a pharmacy fill (OCP and B.C. bylaws, and CBC's report of seven provinces). Rewards on non-Rx shop items only are CAUTION (counsel). Never email a referred friend without their own consent (CASL; consent can't be given on someone else's behalf).

b: Points for purchases. As researched this is not allowed for PEPTICITY. The compliant alternative is in Details.
how: Status without points: a "MEMBER SINCE [YEAR]" card, first access to live sessions, and the Inner List (#21).
risk: STOP on Rx and pharmacy services (Ontario policy; B.C. bylaws upheld). Points on cosmetic or merch purchases only are CAUTION. ---

t: CONSENTED FOLLOW-UP INSTEAD OF PIXEL RETARGETING
b: Follow up on an abandoned quiz or booking, but only with people who gave email consent, and with no health details in the email.
how: "YOU WERE ONE STEP AWAY. HERE'S YOUR LINK TO FINISH." The email holds the link and never the answers. Send at most two, then stop.
risk: CAUTION. PIPEDA express consent; the CASL unsubscribe. Never upload quiz answers or "visited weight page" lists to ad platforms. ---

t: FREE "TALK IT THROUGH" CALL OR FREE ASSESSMENT
b: A no-cost first step.
how: A free 15-minute call with a care coordinator, who isn't a clinician and gives no medical advice, covering process, price and province. The paid clinician consult follows. Booking asks for name, phone, email, province and best time.
risk: CAUTION. Make it clear the coordinator isn't a clinician (AB 489 logic; see the earlier doc). Check whether a free consult counts as an inducement under provincial physician rules [UNVERIFIED].

t: REFUNDABLE BOOKING DEPOSIT, CREDITED TO THE CONSULT
b: A small hold that cuts no-shows and qualifies leads.
how: "$[X] HOLDS YOUR TIME AND COMES OFF YOUR CONSULT FEE. CANCEL [24 H] AHEAD FOR A FULL REFUND." It sits beside the button, not in the terms.
risk: SAFE if it is disclosed up front and included in the all-in price (drip pricing).

b: A three-field form for people who won't book online.
how: "REQUEST A CALL" with name, mobile and province, and a time window (morning, afternoon or evening). The success screen says "[We'll call within X business hours]" (placeholder until true).
risk: SAFE. A call-back request is consent for that call, not for marketing, so add a separate unticked box for the letter. ---

b: An automated series after any signup.
risk: SAFE with the wording rules. Confirm double opt-in for the marketing list ([counsel/owner decision]), and keep consent records per CASL. ---
